# Forced transactions (/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/forced-transactions)

A forced transaction is a message to the child chain that you send through the Delayed Inbox on the parent chain instead of to the sequencer. The message can be a signed transaction, an ETH deposit, a retryable ticket, or an unsigned message. If the sequencer is offline or ignores your message, you can still get it included. After a wait called the force-inclusion window, anyone can move it into the Sequencer Inbox without the sequencer's help.

## Why forced transactions matter [#why-forced-transactions-matter]

The sequencer orders child-chain transactions, so it can delay them. It cannot block them for good. Force inclusion gives every user a path onto the chain that depends only on the parent chain. The one exception is the chain owner, who can [allowlist or pause the Inbox](#things-to-consider).

- **Censorship resistance.** If the sequencer refuses your transaction, you can still get it included.
- **Liveness.** If the sequencer is offline, transactions still reach the chain.
- **A way out.** You can force-include a withdrawal, so you can move funds back to the parent chain without the sequencer. See [Withdraw ETH while the sequencer is down](#withdraw-eth-while-the-sequencer-is-down).
- **Timely disputes on an L3.** On an L3, BoLD assertions and challenge moves go to the parent chain, which is an Arbitrum chain with its own sequencer. If that sequencer censors them, each move waits for force inclusion. The [Censorship Timeout](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/sequencer#censorship-timeout) shortens that wait, so a challenge does not stall for days.

## Key terms [#key-terms]

| Term                                                                              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Delayed Inbox                                     | The parent-chain Inbox contract that accepts messages for the child chain, together with the Bridge contract that records them. Any account can send to it unless the chain owner turns on the Inbox allowlist. Messages wait until the sequencer or a force-inclusion call moves them into the Sequencer Inbox. |
| Sequencer Inbox                                 | The parent-chain contract that holds the canonical, ordered list of child-chain messages. Every child-chain node reads from it.                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Force inclusion                                  | Calling `forceInclusion` on the Sequencer Inbox to move waiting Delayed Inbox messages into the Sequencer Inbox. Anyone can call it once the force-inclusion window has passed.                                                                                                                                                           |
| Force-inclusion window                                                            | How long a Delayed Inbox message must wait before anyone can force-include it. It is the smaller of `delayBlocks` and the delay buffer.                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `delayBlocks`                                                                     | The longest force-inclusion window, in Ethereum blocks. It is one field of the Sequencer Inbox's `maxTimeVariation` setting.                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| [Censorship Timeout](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/sequencer#censorship-timeout) | A Sequencer Inbox feature, also called the delay buffer, that shortens the force-inclusion window after the sequencer has delayed messages for a long time.                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Sequencer feed                                   | The stream the sequencer uses to send new blocks to nodes before it posts them to the parent chain.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

## How a forced transaction works [#how-a-forced-transaction-works]

A forced transaction takes the same path as any other Delayed Inbox message. Only the last step differs.

1. **You send a message to the Delayed Inbox on the parent chain.** Each [message type](#what-you-can-force-include) has its own Inbox function. The parent chain records the message and the block it arrived in.
2. **The sequencer picks it up, or the window runs out.** If the sequencer adds the message, the next batch the batch poster posts to the Sequencer Inbox marks it as read. If the sequencer ignores the message until the force-inclusion window ends, anyone can call `forceInclusion`. It posts an empty batch to the Sequencer Inbox that marks the message as read.
3. **Every child-chain node executes it.** Nodes see the message marked as read in the Sequencer Inbox, take its contents from the Delayed Inbox, and execute it in order.

![A Delayed Inbox message reaches the Sequencer Inbox through the sequencer, or through force inclusion after the window ends](/img/haw-bypassing-the-sequencer.svg)

### When the sequencer is running [#when-the-sequencer-is-running]

When the sequencer is running, you do not need force inclusion. Most transactions go straight to the sequencer through an RPC endpoint. A message you send to the Delayed Inbox also reaches the chain: the sequencer adds it to a child-chain block, and the batch poster later posts that block to the parent chain.

The sequencer's delayed sequencer waits before it adds your message. Sequencer operators turn this component on. By default, it waits until the parent-chain block that holds your message is marked safe. Three [settings](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/blob/ccc5c828d9ea22f161efc784bac4d4a6559b7e59/arbnode/delayed_sequencer.go#L66-L72) change that wait:

- `node.delayed-sequencer.require-full-finality=true` makes it wait for a finalized block instead of a safe one.
- `node.delayed-sequencer.use-merge-finality=false` makes it wait a fixed number of blocks instead.
- `node.delayed-sequencer.finalize-distance` sets that number of blocks, 20 by default. The sequencer also uses this setting if the parent chain does not report safe and finalized blocks.

## What you can force-include [#what-you-can-force-include]

`forceInclusion` works on every Delayed Inbox message, whatever its type. The message type decides which Inbox function you call and what the child chain does with the message.

| Message                                                                                    | Inbox function                                                                     | What the child chain does with it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A signed child-chain transaction                                                           | `sendL2Message` or `sendL2MessageFromOrigin`                                       | Executes it from your own address, with no aliasing. ArbOS drops blob (EIP-4844) transactions. Use this to call any contract or to [withdraw ETH](#withdraw-eth-while-the-sequencer-is-down). The [SDK steps](#force-include-a-signed-transaction-with-the-arbitrum-sdk) use this message type.                                                 |
| An ETH deposit                                                                             | `depositEth`                                                                       | Credits the ETH to the sender's address on the child chain. If a contract sent the deposit, the ETH goes to the contract's aliased address. The [`force-inclusion` example](#runnable-examples) force-includes a deposit.                                                                                                                                               |
| A retryable ticket                                      | `createRetryableTicket`                                                            | Creates the ticket. ArbOS schedules an automatic redemption only if the gas limit is at least 21,000, the fee cap covers the child chain's base fee when the message executes, and the sender's balance covers both. Otherwise, the ticket waits for a manual redemption. See [Retryable tickets](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l1-to-l2-messaging#retryable-tickets). |
| An [unsigned message](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l1-to-l2-messaging#unsigned-messages) | `sendUnsignedTransaction`, `sendContractTransaction`, or their `L1Funded` variants | Executes it from the sender's [aliased address](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l1-to-l2-messaging#address-aliasing).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

For each function's parameters, see [Sending transactions via the Delayed Inbox](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/deposit/eth-and-messages#sending-transactions-via-the-delayed-inbox).

## The force-inclusion timeline [#the-force-inclusion-timeline]

How your message reaches the chain depends on how long the sequencer stays offline or keeps ignoring it.

| How long the sequencer is offline or ignores your message | What happens to your message                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Not at all                                                | The sequencer adds it once the parent-chain block is safe, by default. See [When the sequencer is running](#when-the-sequencer-is-running). |
| Less than the force-inclusion window                      | It waits in the Delayed Inbox. When the sequencer returns, it adds the message in order. Nobody can force-include it yet.                   |
| Longer than the force-inclusion window                    | Anyone can call `forceInclusion`. The message enters the Sequencer Inbox, and every child-chain node processes it.                          |

### Before the window ends [#before-the-window-ends]

Your message is safe in the Delayed Inbox, but only the sequencer can move it. The Sequencer Inbox reverts any `forceInclusion` call for this message with `ForceIncludeBlockTooSoon`. If the sequencer or someone else already included the message, the call reverts earlier, with `DelayedBackwards`.

The sequencer cannot skip or reorder Delayed Inbox messages. It must process them in the order they arrived.

### After the window ends [#after-the-window-ends]

The [`forceInclusion`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-contracts/blob/4341b132cfbdcc980ead03765ca5224ff6cb5d97/src/bridge/SequencerInbox.sol#L273-L330) function succeeds once the current parent-chain block number exceeds your message's block number plus the force-inclusion window.

One call includes your message and every earlier message still waiting in the Delayed Inbox. If someone else force-includes a later message, your message is included too.

> **The contract counts blocks, not seconds**
>
> `forceInclusion` checks only parent-chain block numbers. `delayBlocks` is 7200 Ethereum blocks on Arbitrum One and 7200 on Arbitrum Nova. At 12 seconds per block, that is 24 hours and 24 hours.
>
> If the parent chain is itself an Arbitrum chain, as it is for an L3, `block.number` returns the parent chain's estimate of the Ethereum block number. The parent chain's sequencer sets that value, and it stays close to the real Ethereum block number. The window is counted in these Ethereum block numbers. See [Block numbers and time](/arbitrum-essentials/arbitrum-vs-ethereum/block-numbers-and-time#ethereum-or-parent-chain-block-numbers-within-arbitrum).
>
> The parent chain's `block.number` advances only when the parent chain produces blocks. If the parent chain's own sequencer is also down, the L3's window stops advancing until the parent chain produces blocks again.

### When a force inclusion reorders the chain [#when-a-force-inclusion-reorders-the-chain]

A force inclusion can cause a reorg on the child chain. This happens when the sequencer produced blocks it never posted to the parent chain. Those blocks were soft-confirmed through the sequencer feed, but the force-included messages now come before them in the Sequencer Inbox.

Every node that follows the sequencer feed reorgs as soon as it reads the empty batch that `forceInclusion` posts to the Sequencer Inbox. It drops the unposted blocks. Soft-confirmed transactions in those blocks can be lost for good:

- **Only an active sequencer re-sequences.** If the sequencer isn't active when the reorg happens, it doesn't re-sequence the dropped messages.
- **Re-sequencing has a depth limit.** The sequencer re-sequences up to 1,024 dropped messages by default (`node.transaction-streamer.max-reorg-resequence-depth`). It removes any messages beyond that limit.
- **Re-sequencing is best effort.** The sequencer skips any message it fails to re-sequence and moves on to the next one.
- **Re-sequenced transactions can fail.** The chain state changes underneath them, so some revert or are dropped.

> **A reorg happens on each node, not on the whole chain**
>
> Only nodes that follow the sequencer feed see the unposted blocks, so only they reorg. A node that reads only from the parent chain builds blocks from posted batches, already in canonical order. It never reorgs because of a force inclusion. It can still follow a parent-chain reorg unless you set `node.inbox-reader.read-mode` to `safe` or `finalized`, which also turns off the feed. In exchange, it sees transactions only after they're posted, not when they're soft-confirmed.

### How the Censorship Timeout shortens the window [#how-the-censorship-timeout-shortens-the-window]

The force-inclusion window is the smaller of `delayBlocks` and the delay buffer. Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova both have the delay buffer enabled.

- **The buffer starts full.** The maximum is 14,400 Ethereum blocks (48 hours). While the buffer is at least `delayBlocks`, the window is `delayBlocks`: 24 hours on Arbitrum One and 24 hours on Arbitrum Nova.
- **Long delays drain the buffer.** If the sequencer delays a Delayed Inbox message past a `threshold`, the extra delay comes out of the buffer. The `threshold` is 150 blocks (30 minutes) on Arbitrum One and 300 blocks (1 hour) on Arbitrum Nova.
- **Draining is capped and applied later.** The contract records a delay when it updates the buffer and deducts it at the next update. Each deduction is at most the number of blocks between the two updates.
- **The buffer never drops below the threshold.** So the shortest possible window is 30 minutes on Arbitrum One and 1 hour on Arbitrum Nova.
- **The buffer refills slowly.** At each update, the contract adds 5% of the blocks elapsed since the last update, then deducts any recorded delay. That is about one day of buffer for every 20 days without long delays.

The first force-included message of an outage gets the full `delayBlocks` window, as long as the buffer holds at least `delayBlocks` when the outage starts. That force inclusion records a delay of about `delayBlocks` blocks. Later messages in the same long outage pay for it, so their windows get shorter. Repeated outages drain the buffer the same way. For the full math, see the [`DelayBuffer` library](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-contracts/blob/4341b132cfbdcc980ead03765ca5224ff6cb5d97/src/bridge/DelayBuffer.sol) and the [Censorship Timeout](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/sequencer#censorship-timeout) section.

### Window settings on Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova [#window-settings-on-arbitrum-one-and-arbitrum-nova]

Block counts are Ethereum blocks, at 12 seconds per block.

| Setting                               | Arbitrum One                                                                                              | Arbitrum Nova                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `delayBlocks`, the longest window     | 7200 blocks (24 hours) | 7200 blocks (24 hours) |
| Largest delay buffer                  | 14,400 blocks (48 hours)                                                                                  | 14,400 blocks (48 hours)                                                                              |
| `threshold`, also the shortest window | 150 blocks (30 minutes)                                                                                   | 300 blocks (1 hour)                                                                                   |
| Buffer refill rate                    | 5% of elapsed blocks                                                                                      | 5% of elapsed blocks                                                                                  |

To get the deadline for a message, call [`forceInclusionDeadline(blockNumber)`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-contracts/blob/4341b132cfbdcc980ead03765ca5224ff6cb5d97/src/bridge/SequencerInbox.sol#L755-L764) on the Sequencer Inbox. It applies the buffer's pending changes for you. You can force-include from the block after the deadline it returns.

The deadline can move. A sequencer batch or another force inclusion updates the buffer, which changes the result. Call `forceInclusionDeadline` again right before you call `forceInclusion`.

## Force-include a signed transaction with the Arbitrum SDK [#force-include-a-signed-transaction-with-the-arbitrum-sdk]

These steps send a signed child-chain transaction with `sendL2Message` and force-include it. To force-include another message type, replace steps 2 and 3 with that type's [Inbox function](#what-you-can-force-include). Steps 4 and 5 work the same for every type. Step 6 finds the result by the signed transaction's hash, so it applies only to signed transactions.

The steps use the [`InboxTools`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-sdk/blob/cbb96c6f7f84d71bdef65d0fd9d3d7275a236711/packages/sdk/src/lib/inbox/inbox.ts#L64) class from `@arbitrum/sdk` v4 with ethers v5.

You need:

- An account with ETH on the parent chain to pay for the parent-chain transactions.
- The same account with enough funds on the child chain to pay for the child-chain transaction.
- An RPC endpoint for the parent chain.
- An RPC endpoint for a child-chain node that reads from the parent chain. A full node works. It doesn't need the sequencer or the sequencer feed.

### 1. Set up the SDK [#1-set-up-the-sdk]

```ts
import { providers, Wallet, Contract, utils } from 'ethers';
import { getArbitrumNetwork, InboxTools } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(process.env.PARENT_CHAIN_RPC);
const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(process.env.CHAIN_RPC);

const parentWallet = new Wallet(process.env.PRIVATE_KEY, parentProvider);
const childWallet = new Wallet(process.env.PRIVATE_KEY, childProvider);

const childNetwork = await getArbitrumNetwork(childProvider);
const inboxTools = new InboxTools(parentWallet, childNetwork);
```

`getArbitrumNetwork` knows Arbitrum One, Arbitrum Nova, and Arbitrum Sepolia out of the box. If your chain is not one of them, call `registerCustomArbitrumNetwork` with your chain's details first. Otherwise, `getArbitrumNetwork` throws `Unrecognized network`.

### 2. Sign the child-chain transaction [#2-sign-the-child-chain-transaction]

`signChildTx` fills in the nonce and fees from the child-chain node if you leave them out. It always sets the gas limit to the node's current estimate, with no margin. Then it signs the transaction with your child-chain wallet.

```ts
const feeData = await childProvider.getFeeData();

const signedTx = await inboxTools.signChildTx(
  {
    to: '0xRecipientAddress',
    value: utils.parseEther('0.01'),
    data: '0x',
    // Leave room for the base fee to rise before the transaction executes
    maxFeePerGas: feeData.maxFeePerGas.mul(3),
    maxPriorityFeePerGas: 0,
  },
  childWallet,
);

// Save this hash to find the transaction on the child chain later
const childTxHash = utils.parseTransaction(signedTx).hash;
```

The fee cap and gas limit are fixed once you sign. Your transaction might execute a day or more later, so set `maxFeePerGas` well above today's base fee. If the transaction's gas use depends on chain state that can change, sign it with ethers directly and set a higher gas limit yourself.

### 3. Send it to the Delayed Inbox [#3-send-it-to-the-delayed-inbox]

`sendChildSignedTx` calls `sendL2Message` on the Delayed Inbox. Because the message is signed, the child chain executes it from your own address, with no [address aliasing](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l1-to-l2-messaging#address-aliasing).

```ts
const parentTx = await inboxTools.sendChildSignedTx(signedTx);
const parentReceipt = await parentTx.wait();
```

If the sequencer is running, it adds your transaction without force inclusion. Skip to step 6.

### 4. Wait for the force-inclusion deadline [#4-wait-for-the-force-inclusion-deadline]

Ask the Sequencer Inbox for your message's deadline. The result includes pending changes in the delay buffer.

```ts
const sequencerInbox = new Contract(childNetwork.ethBridge.sequencerInbox, ['function forceInclusionDeadline(uint64 blockNumber) view returns (uint64)'], parentProvider);

const deadline = await sequencerInbox.forceInclusionDeadline(parentReceipt.blockNumber);
console.log(`Force inclusion opens after parent-chain block ${deadline}`);
```

Wait until the parent chain's block number is greater than `deadline`. Then check the deadline again, because a later batch can move it.

If your parent chain is an Arbitrum chain, both numbers are Ethereum block numbers, not the parent chain's own block numbers. The plain ethers receipt doesn't include the Ethereum block number. Read both numbers through the SDK's `ArbitrumProvider` instead:

```ts
import { ArbitrumProvider } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const arbParentProvider = new ArbitrumProvider(parentProvider);

// The Ethereum block number your message was recorded at
const messageReceipt = await arbParentProvider.getTransactionReceipt(parentReceipt.transactionHash);
const l3Deadline = await sequencerInbox.forceInclusionDeadline(messageReceipt.l1BlockNumber);

// Compare against this, not against parentProvider.getBlockNumber()
const currentBlock = await arbParentProvider.getBlock('latest');
const isOpen = currentBlock.l1BlockNumber > l3Deadline.toNumber();
```

### 5. Force-include the message [#5-force-include-the-message]

Pass your own message to `forceInclude`. Take the `MessageDelivered` event from your step 3 receipt, and read the message's accumulator from the Bridge contract.

```ts
import { ParentTransactionReceipt } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const bridge = new Contract(childNetwork.ethBridge.bridge, ['function delayedInboxAccs(uint256 index) view returns (bytes32)'], parentProvider);

// The MessageDelivered event your step 3 transaction emitted
const [delivered] = new ParentTransactionReceipt(parentReceipt).getMessageDeliveredEvents();

const forceTx = await inboxTools.forceInclude({
  event: delivered,
  blockNumber: parentReceipt.blockNumber,
  blockHash: parentReceipt.blockHash,
  delayedAcc: await bridge.delayedInboxAccs(delivered.messageIndex),
} as any); // forceInclude reads only these fields
await forceTx.wait();
```

The call includes your message and every earlier message still waiting. If your parent chain is an Arbitrum chain, `forceInclude` converts the block number to an Ethereum block number for you. If the sequencer or someone else already included your message, the call reverts with `DelayedBackwards`.

> **Calling forceInclude() with no arguments can miss your message**
>
> With no arguments, `forceInclude` searches the parent chain for the newest eligible message. The search is stricter than the contract:
>
> - It treats a message as eligible only after both `delayBlocks` and `delaySeconds` have passed.
> - It ignores the delay buffer. If the buffer has shortened the window, it misses messages the contract already accepts.
> - It searches back at most 19,635 blocks (`3 * 6545`, about three days) from the newest eligible block. It misses older messages.
>
> In these cases it returns `null`, even though your window is open. Use the no-argument form only when you don't have your message's receipt.

### 6. Confirm the transaction on the child chain [#6-confirm-the-transaction-on-the-child-chain]

The child-chain node reads the force-included message from the Sequencer Inbox and processes it. Wait with a timeout, because an invalid transaction never gets a receipt.

```ts
// Wait up to 30 minutes for one confirmation
const childReceipt = await childProvider.waitForTransaction(childTxHash, 1, 30 * 60 * 1000).catch(() => null);

if (childReceipt === null) {
  console.log('No receipt. ArbOS may have dropped the transaction; see "When a signed transaction has no receipt".');
} else {
  console.log(`Child-chain status: ${childReceipt.status === 1 ? 'success' : 'reverted'}`);
}
```

For other message types, start from the same step 3 receipt. Wrap it with `new ParentTransactionReceipt(parentReceipt)`, then:

- **ETH deposit.** Call `getEthDeposits(childProvider)`, then `wait()` on the result.
- **Retryable ticket.** Call `getParentToChildMessages(childProvider)`, then `waitForStatus()` on the result.

### Withdraw ETH while the sequencer is down [#withdraw-eth-while-the-sequencer-is-down]

To move ETH back to the parent chain without the sequencer, force-include a call to the `ArbSys` precompile's `withdrawEth` method. [`ArbSys`](/arbitrum-essentials/precompiles/reference#arbsys) lives at address `0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000064`.

In step 2, sign this transaction instead:

```ts
const arbSys = new utils.Interface(['function withdrawEth(address destination) payable returns (uint256)']);

const signedTx = await inboxTools.signChildTx(
  {
    to: '0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000064',
    // The ETH to withdraw from your child-chain balance
    value: utils.parseEther('0.1'),
    // The parent-chain address that receives the ETH
    data: arbSys.encodeFunctionData('withdrawEth', [parentWallet.address]),
    maxFeePerGas: feeData.maxFeePerGas.mul(3),
    maxPriorityFeePerGas: 0,
  },
  childWallet,
);
```

Then follow steps 3 through 6. When the transaction lands, the child chain burns your ETH and creates a child-to-parent message. Claim the ETH on the parent chain after the challenge period: 6.4 days on Arbitrum One and 6.4 days on Arbitrum Nova. See [Withdrawing ETH](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages#withdrawing-eth) for the claim steps.

### Runnable examples [#runnable-examples]

- [`delayedInbox-l2msg`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-tutorials/tree/master/packages/delayedInbox-l2msg) sends a signed transaction through the Delayed Inbox while the sequencer is running.
- [`force-inclusion`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-tutorials/tree/master/packages/force-inclusion) deploys a test chain with a 90-second window, deposits ETH, and force-includes the deposit with no sequencer.

## When a signed transaction has no receipt [#when-a-signed-transaction-has-no-receipt]

Force inclusion guarantees that every child-chain node processes your message. It does not guarantee that a signed transaction executes. ArbOS checks a signed transaction before it executes it. If a check fails, ArbOS drops the transaction, and the transaction hash never gets a receipt.

| What went wrong                                                                               | Result                            |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| The nonce no longer matches, because you sent another transaction from the same account first | Dropped, no receipt               |
| The child chain's base fee rose above your `maxFeePerGas`                                     | Dropped, no receipt               |
| Your child-chain balance cannot cover the gas limit times the fee, plus the value             | Dropped, no receipt               |
| The signature or chain ID is wrong, or the message cannot be parsed                           | Dropped, no receipt               |
| The transaction passes these checks but runs out of gas or reverts                            | Included, receipt with `status` 0 |

If you get no receipt, check the account's current nonce and balance on the child chain. Compare the current base fee with the fee cap you signed. Then sign a new transaction and resend it. ArbOS records the reason only in the node's log, at debug level, or at warn level on a chain in debug mode.

## Things to consider [#things-to-consider]

- **A signed transaction's nonce is fixed when you sign.** Wait until the forced transaction lands before you send another child-chain transaction from the same account.
- **A signed transaction's fee cap and gas limit are fixed when you sign.** Set both with room to spare, as described in step 2.
- **You pay parent-chain gas twice.** You pay once to send the message and again for `forceInclusion`. Signed transactions, unsigned messages, and retryable tickets also pay child-chain gas.
- **An Inbox allowlist limits who can send.** A chain owner can turn on the Inbox allowlist with `setAllowListEnabled`. The Inbox then checks the account that signed the parent-chain transaction (`tx.origin`), so only allowlisted accounts can send messages to the Delayed Inbox. Other accounts cannot start a forced transaction.
- **A paused Inbox accepts no messages.** The chain owner can pause the Inbox, and every send function reverts while it is paused. Messages already in the Delayed Inbox can still be force-included, because `forceInclusion` is on the Sequencer Inbox. See [Ownership and access](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/ownership-and-access#inbox-delayed-inbox).
- **Each chain sets its own window.** The numbers on this page are for Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova. If you run your own Arbitrum chain, it can use different values. See [Sequencer timing adjustments](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/sequencer/sequencer-timing-adjustments).

## Example scenario [#example-scenario]

Suppose the Arbitrum One sequencer goes offline while its delay buffer is full.

1. **Monday, 12:00 UTC.** You send a signed transaction to the Delayed Inbox. The parent chain records it in Ethereum block `N`.
2. **Monday, 18:00 UTC.** The sequencer is still offline. A call to `forceInclusion` reverts with `ForceIncludeBlockTooSoon`.
3. **Tuesday, about 12:00 UTC.** Ethereum reaches the block after `N` + 7200. You call `forceInclusion`, and your message enters the Sequencer Inbox.
4. **Tuesday, a few minutes later.** Child-chain full nodes read the new inbox entry and process your transaction. If it passes the ArbOS checks, your receipt appears on the child chain.
5. **Later.** The sequencer comes back online. It continues from the force-included messages. Every node that follows the sequencer feed has already dropped the blocks the sequencer produced but never posted, and the sequencer tries to re-sequence them.

If the sequencer had come back on Monday evening, it would have included your message, and you wouldn't have needed step 3.

## Related pages [#related-pages]

- [Transaction lifecycle: bypassing the sequencer](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/transaction-lifecycle#bypassing-the-sequencer)
- [Parent to child chain messaging: transacting via the Delayed Inbox](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l1-to-l2-messaging#transacting-via-the-delayed-inbox)
- [The sequencer and censorship resistance](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/sequencer)
- [Sequencer timing adjustments](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/sequencer/sequencer-timing-adjustments)
- [How to bridge from child chain to parent chain](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages)

[#compare-provider-latency] To compare the live latency of the public Arbitrum endpoints that need no API key, use the [OpenChainBench Arbitrum RPC benchmark](https://openchainbench.com/benchmarks/arbitrum-rpc). OpenChainBench probes each endpoint every minute from three regions. It publishes the p50, p95, and p99 latency under an open methodology and the CC BY 4.0 license. ## Sequencer endpoint behavior [#sequencer-endpoint-behavior] Arbitrum One has two public endpoints with different roles. The public RPC URL is for general use. The direct sequencer endpoint accepts only `eth_sendRawTransaction` and `eth_sendRawTransactionConditional`. The table compares their purpose and operational guarantees. ### The two endpoints at a glance [#the-two-endpoints-at-a-glance] | Endpoint | Purpose | Operational guarantees | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **`https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc` (public RPC URL)** | General-purpose read/write endpoint, useful for development and low-volume reads. | **No uptime, latency, or rate-limit guarantees.** If your decentralized app depends on availability, use a third-party node provider or run your own node. | | **`https://arb1-sequencer.arbitrum.io/rpc` (sequencer endpoint)** | Direct submission path to the chain's sequencer for write traffic. Accepts only `eth_sendRawTransaction` and `eth_sendRawTransactionConditional`. | Has the queueing and timeout behavior described below. It is still a best-effort public endpoint with no formal service-level agreement (SLA). | ### Latency and timeout behavior [#latency-and-timeout-behavior] Under normal load, the sequencer endpoint accepts a transaction in less than a second. The sequencer puts each submission in a bounded in-memory queue. By default, the queue holds 1,024 transactions. The queue timeout is 12 seconds by default. It limits how long a transaction can wait in the queue before the sequencer picks it up or rejects it. The timeout is **not** an end-to-end inclusion latency guarantee. If the sequencer does not pick up the transaction before the timeout, `eth_sendRawTransaction` returns `context deadline exceeded`. In that case, the sequencer did **not** accept the transaction, and you can safely retry it. ### Recommended fallback patterns [#recommended-fallback-patterns] - Use a third-party node provider as your primary endpoint, or as a fallback when a direct sequencer submission fails. - Retry only on transient errors. You can safely retry `context deadline exceeded` and network or connection errors with backoff. Do not retry terminal errors, such as `nonce too low` or contract reverts. ### Monitoring and alerting [#monitoring-and-alerting] A successful `eth_sendRawTransaction` response means that the sequencer has already put your transaction in an L2 block. The call returns only after the sequencer creates the block, not when it adds the transaction to the queue. Treat this response as the sequencer's soft confirmation: the sequencer has ordered and executed your transaction. The response does **not** mean that the transaction is posted in a batch to the parent chain, or final there. If your app needs parent-chain finality, track it separately. For monitoring, alert on submission calls that return errors or take longer than your latency limit. Do not assume a pending-but-unconfirmed state. === https://docs.arbitrum.io/arbitrum-bridge/withdrawal-monitoring.md (200) === # Monitor withdrawals programmatically (/arbitrum-bridge/withdrawal-monitoring) This page is intended for chain operators and integration partners (exchanges, bridges, infrastructure providers) who need to track withdrawals programmatically and be alerted when one gets stuck. To trace a single transaction end to end, see [Tracing bridge transactions](/arbitrum-bridge/bridge-transaction-traceability). To initiate withdrawals from code, see [Withdraw ETH and messages](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages). To learn the protocol-level background, see [Child-to-parent messaging](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l2-to-l1-messaging). A withdrawal from an Arbitrum chain is a child chain-to-parent chain message that passes through several protocol stages before funds are claimable. Most "where is my withdrawal?" questions come down to not knowing which stage a withdrawal is in, or how long each stage is expected to take on a given chain. This guide maps the lifecycle to observable onchain state and to the [`@arbitrum/sdk`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-sdk) status model, gives expected timelines per chain type, and provides tested code for monitoring one withdrawal or indexing many. ## The withdrawal lifecycle [#the-withdrawal-lifecycle] Every withdrawal—whether a token withdrawal through the bridge UI or a raw `ArbSys.sendTxToL1` call—moves through the same stages: | Stage | What happens onchain | SDK status | | :--------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------ | | **1. Initiated** | The child chain transaction calls the [`ArbSys`](/arbitrum-essentials/precompiles/reference#arbsys) precompile (directly, or via a token gateway), which emits an `L2ToL1Tx` event containing the withdrawal's `position` | `UNCONFIRMED` | | **2. Batched** | The sequencer posts the batch containing the transaction to the parent chain (typically within minutes) | `UNCONFIRMED` | | **3. Asserted** | A validator posts an assertion covering the withdrawal's child chain block (`AssertionCreated` event on the Rollup contract) | `UNCONFIRMED` | | **4. Confirmed** | After the challenge period passes without a successful challenge, the assertion is confirmed (`AssertionConfirmed` event); the Rollup contract registers the assertion's send root in the outbox (`SendRootUpdated` event) | `CONFIRMED` | | **5. Executed** | Someone calls `Outbox.executeTransaction()` with a Merkle proof (obtained from a child chain node via `NodeInterface.constructOutboxProof()`);; the outbox marks the withdrawal spent (`OutBoxTransactionExecuted` event) and releases the funds | `EXECUTED` | Two properties of this lifecycle cause most confusion: - **Execution is manual.** Confirmation makes a withdrawal _claimable_; it doesn't deliver funds. Someone (the user through the bridge UI's **Claim** button, or your infrastructure) must execute the claim on the parent chain. A withdrawal can sit in `CONFIRMED` indefinitely. To learn why the protocol works this way, see [Why child to parent chain messages require manual execution](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l2-to-l1-messaging#why-child-to-parent-chain-messages-require-manual-execution). - **Time-to-claimable is more than the challenge period.** The clock users care about includes batch posting (minutes) _plus_ waiting for the next assertion to cover their block (up to the chain's assertion posting interval, commonly up to an hour) _plus_ the challenge period after that assertion is created. On a chain with [fast withdrawals](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/fast-withdrawals), the committee's confirmation frequency replaces the challenge period wait, but batch posting and assertion cadence still apply—which is why a "15-minute fast withdrawal chain" can legitimately take an hour or more to reach claimable. ### Mapping bridge UI phases to protocol states [#mapping-bridge-ui-phases-to-protocol-states] The [Arbitrum bridge UI](https://bridge.arbitrum.io/) presents a withdrawal as three user-facing steps, and support conversations often reference them as "phases." They map to the lifecycle above as follows: | Bridge UI step | Lifecycle stages | SDK status | | :------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------- | :----------------------- | | Phase 1 — withdrawal submitted | Initiated | `UNCONFIRMED` | | Phase 2 — countdown or waiting | Batched → Asserted → challenge period elapsing | `UNCONFIRMED` | | Phase 3 — **Claim** button available, then claimed | Confirmed → Executed | `CONFIRMED` → `EXECUTED` | A withdrawal "stuck between phase 2 and phase 3" is a withdrawal that stayed `UNCONFIRMED` past its expected time-to-claimable: either no assertion covering its block exists yet, or the covering assertion hasn't been confirmed. The [diagnosis table](#diagnose-stuck-withdrawals) below separates those cases. ## Expected timelines by chain type [#expected-timelines-by-chain-type] The dominant term in time-to-claimable is the challenge period, set by the chain's `confirmPeriodBlocks` parameter and measured in parent chain blocks. Values for Arbitrum's own chains: | Chain configuration | Challenge period | Typical time-to-claimable | | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Arbitrum One (Rollup) | 45818 blocks ≈ 6.4 days | ~7 days (batch + assertion cadence + challenge period) | | Arbitrum Nova (AnyTrust) | 45818 blocks ≈ 6.4 days | ~7 days—AnyTrust changes data availability, **not** the challenge period | | Arbitrum chain with fast withdrawals | Bypassed by unanimous committee confirmation | As low as ~15 minutes on BoLD-enabled chains, plus batch posting and assertion cadence | | Arbitrum Sepolia (testnet) | 20 blocks ≈ 4.0 minutes | Minutes | Additional timing facts your alerting thresholds should account for: - **A challenged assertion takes longer.** If an assertion acquires a rival, confirmation waits for the challenge to resolve (bounded by the challenge period) plus a grace period (14,400 parent chain blocks ≈ 48 hours on Arbitrum One's configuration) before the winner can be confirmed. Under BoLD, an honest withdrawal is delayed by at most one additional challenge period even during a dispute—see [Assertions](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/assertions). - **Time-to-funds = time-to-claimable + execution.** Budget for the claim transaction separately; nothing executes it automatically. - **Custom chains choose their own values.** Read `confirmPeriodBlocks()` from the chain's Rollup contract (shown [below](#query-assertion-and-outbox-state-onchain)) rather than assuming the defaults. To learn how operators configure this, see [Customizable challenge period](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/challenge-period). ## Withdrawals from an L3 [#withdrawals-from-an-l3] A withdrawal from an L3 (an Arbitrum chain that settles on Arbitrum One or another child chain) to Ethereum is **two sequential child-to-parent withdrawals**: L3 → L2, then L2 → L1. Each leg has its own challenge period—by default 45818 parent chain blocks (≈ 6.4 days) per leg on mainnet configurations—and each leg's claim must execute before the next leg can begin. The worst case with default settings is therefore roughly two weeks end to end. Monitor each leg independently with the same code from this guide, pointing the provider pair at the relevant chains (L3 + L2 for the first leg, L2 + L1 for the second). Chain operators have three options for reducing the delay: | Option | Time-to-claimable | Trade-off | | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [Fast withdrawals](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/fast-withdrawals) | Down to ~15 minutes per leg on BoLD-enabled chains | Adds a committee trust assumption (unanimous validator committee); recommended primarily for AnyTrust chains where the DAC already exists | | [Customizable challenge period](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/challenge-period) | Whatever `confirmPeriodBlocks` is set to | Shrinks the window in which fraud can be challenged; weakens the chain's security model | | Third-party liquidity bridges | Minutes | Users receive funds from a liquidity provider rather than the canonical bridge; adds provider trust and fees; per-asset liquidity limits | ## Monitor withdrawals with the SDK [#monitor-withdrawals-with-the-sdk] The [`@arbitrum/sdk`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-sdk) (v4, ethers v5) exposes the lifecycle through `ChildToParentMessage` objects and the `ChildToParentMessageStatus` enum, whose three values match the lifecycle table above: `UNCONFIRMED` (0), `CONFIRMED` (1), and `EXECUTED` (2). The SDK handles both current (BoLD) and legacy assertion models automatically, so the same code works across chains. Arbitrum One, Nova, and Arbitrum Sepolia are pre-registered in the SDK. For any other Arbitrum chain, register it first—all required parameters can be derived from the chain's Rollup contract address: ```ts import { providers } from 'ethers'; import { registerCustomArbitrumNetwork, getArbitrumNetworkInformationFromRollup } from '@arbitrum/sdk'; const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL); const rollupData = await getArbitrumNetworkInformationFromRollup(ROLLUP_ADDRESS, parentProvider); registerCustomArbitrumNetwork({ chainId: CHILD_CHAIN_ID, name: 'my-arbitrum-chain', parentChainId: rollupData.parentChainId, ethBridge: rollupData.ethBridge, confirmPeriodBlocks: rollupData.confirmPeriodBlocks, isCustom: true, isTestnet: false, }); ``` ### Check the status of a withdrawal [#check-the-status-of-a-withdrawal] Given the withdrawal's child chain transaction hash: ```ts import { providers } from 'ethers'; import { ChildTransactionReceipt, ChildToParentMessageStatus } from '@arbitrum/sdk'; const withdrawalTxHash = WITHDRAWAL_TX_HASH; const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL); const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL); async function main() { const receipt = await childProvider.getTransactionReceipt(withdrawalTxHash); const childReceipt = new ChildTransactionReceipt(receipt); const messages = await childReceipt.getChildToParentMessages(parentProvider); const message = messages[0]; const status = await message.status(childProvider); console.log('Status:', ChildToParentMessageStatus[status]); if (status === ChildToParentMessageStatus.UNCONFIRMED) { // Estimated parent chain block at which the withdrawal becomes executable const firstExecutableBlock = await message.getFirstExecutableBlock(childProvider); console.log('Estimated first executable parent chain block:', firstExecutableBlock.toString()); } } main(); ``` `getFirstExecutableBlock()` returns an estimate of the parent chain block at which the message becomes claimable (based on the covering assertion's creation block plus the challenge period), or `null` once the message is already `CONFIRMED` or `EXECUTED`. Comparing it against the parent chain's current block number gives you a countdown you can surface to users—the same countdown the bridge UI shows. ### Wait for confirmation and execute the claim [#wait-for-confirmation-and-execute-the-claim] `waitUntilReadyToExecute()` polls until the message leaves `UNCONFIRMED`, then returns the terminal status. A `ChildToParentMessageWriter` (obtained by passing a parent chain _signer_ instead of a provider) can then execute the claim: ```ts import { providers, Wallet } from 'ethers'; import { ChildTransactionReceipt, ChildToParentMessageStatus } from '@arbitrum/sdk'; const withdrawalTxHash = WITHDRAWAL_TX_HASH; const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL); const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL); const parentSigner = new Wallet(PRIVATE_KEY, parentProvider); async function main() { const receipt = await childProvider.getTransactionReceipt(withdrawalTxHash); const childReceipt = new ChildTransactionReceipt(receipt); // Passing a signer yields ChildToParentMessageWriter instances, which can execute claims const messages = await childReceipt.getChildToParentMessages(parentSigner); const message = messages[0]; // Polls every 30 seconds until the message leaves UNCONFIRMED. // On a chain with a live challenge period this call blocks for days — // use it in a worker, or poll status() on your own schedule instead. const status = await message.waitUntilReadyToExecute(childProvider, 30 * 1000); if (status === ChildToParentMessageStatus.CONFIRMED) { const executeTx = await message.execute(childProvider); const executeReceipt = await executeTx.wait(); console.log('Claim executed on parent chain:', executeReceipt.transactionHash); } else { console.log('Message already executed'); } } main(); ``` Under the hood, `execute()` fetches the Merkle proof from the [`NodeInterface`](/arbitrum-essentials/nodeinterface/reference) and calls `Outbox.executeTransaction()` on the parent chain. It throws if the message isn't `CONFIRMED` yet. If you need the proof itself (for example, to execute through your own contracts), call `message.getOutboxProof(childProvider)`. ### Index many withdrawals [#index-many-withdrawals] To monitor every withdrawal on a chain (for example, all withdrawals initiated through your bridge frontend), fetch `L2ToL1Tx` events in bulk instead of tracking individual transaction hashes: ```ts import { providers } from 'ethers'; import { ChildToParentMessage, ChildToParentMessageStatus } from '@arbitrum/sdk'; const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL); const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL); const fromBlock = START_BLOCK; const toBlock = 'latest'; async function main() { const events = await ChildToParentMessage.getChildToParentEvents(childProvider, { fromBlock, toBlock, }); console.log(`Found ${events.length} withdrawal(s)`); for (const event of events) { const message = ChildToParentMessage.fromEvent(parentProvider, event); const status = await message.status(childProvider); console.log(`position ${event.position.toString()} | ` + `child tx ${event.transactionHash} | ` + `destination ${event.destination} | ` + `${ChildToParentMessageStatus[status]}`); } } main(); ``` `getChildToParentEvents` also accepts optional `position`, `destination`, and `hash` filters (all indexed fields of the `L2ToL1Tx` event), so you can restrict the scan to withdrawals bound for addresses you care about. For a production monitor, a practical pattern is: 1. **Ingest**: scan `L2ToL1Tx` events in block-range windows on a schedule; store each withdrawal's `position`, transaction hash, destination, and initiation timestamp. 2. **Track**: poll `status()` for stored withdrawals that aren't `EXECUTED` yet. Withdrawals in `UNCONFIRMED` only change state when an assertion is confirmed, so polling them more often than the chain's assertion cadence adds no information; hourly is plenty on a seven-day chain. 3. **Alert**: flag any withdrawal that is `UNCONFIRMED` past your chain's expected time-to-claimable (challenge period + assertion cadence + margin), and any withdrawal sitting in `CONFIRMED` longer than you expect users to leave claims unexecuted. ## Query assertion and outbox state onchain [#query-assertion-and-outbox-state-onchain] If you prefer raw contract calls—or want to monitor the assertion pipeline itself rather than individual messages—the same lifecycle is observable from three contracts: the `ArbSys` precompile on the child chain, and the Rollup and Outbox contracts on the parent chain. The following snippet checks every stage for one withdrawal: ```ts import { providers, Contract } from 'ethers'; const withdrawalTxHash = WITHDRAWAL_TX_HASH; const rollupAddress = ROLLUP_ADDRESS; const ARBSYS_ADDRESS = '0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000064'; const NODE_INTERFACE_ADDRESS = '0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000C8'; const arbSysAbi = ['event L2ToL1Tx(address caller, address indexed destination, uint256 indexed hash, uint256 indexed position, uint256 arbBlockNum, uint256 ethBlockNum, uint256 timestamp, uint256 callvalue, bytes data)']; const rollupAbi = ['function outbox() view returns (address)', 'function confirmPeriodBlocks() view returns (uint64)', 'event AssertionConfirmed(bytes32 indexed assertionHash, bytes32 blockHash, bytes32 sendRoot)']; const outboxAbi = ['function roots(bytes32) view returns (bytes32)', 'function isSpent(uint256 index) view returns (bool)']; const nodeInterfaceAbi = ['function constructOutboxProof(uint64 size, uint64 leaf) view returns (bytes32 send, bytes32 root, bytes32[] proof)']; const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL); const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL); async function main() { // 1. The L2ToL1Tx event from the withdrawal transaction identifies the message const receipt = await childProvider.getTransactionReceipt(withdrawalTxHash); const arbSys = new Contract(ARBSYS_ADDRESS, arbSysAbi, childProvider); const l2ToL1TxTopic = arbSys.interface.getEventTopic('L2ToL1Tx'); const event = receipt.logs.filter((log) => log.topics[0] === l2ToL1TxTopic).map((log) => arbSys.interface.parseLog(log))[0]; const { position, arbBlockNum } = event.args; console.log('position (outbox leaf index):', position.toString(), '| child block:', arbBlockNum.toString()); // 2. Latest confirmed assertion: its send root commits to all withdrawals up to // the child chain block it covers const rollup = new Contract(rollupAddress, rollupAbi, parentProvider); const confirmed = await rollup.queryFilter(rollup.filters.AssertionConfirmed(), -100000); const latestConfirmation = confirmed[confirmed.length - 1]; const { blockHash, sendRoot } = latestConfirmation.args; // 3. sendCount of that block = how many withdrawals the confirmed assertion covers const confirmedBlock = await childProvider.send('eth_getBlockByHash', [blockHash, false]); const sendCount = Number(confirmedBlock.sendCount); const isCovered = position.lt(sendCount); console.log('confirmed sendCount:', sendCount, '| withdrawal covered by confirmed assertion:', isCovered); // 4. The send root must be registered in the outbox for claims to succeed const outboxAddress = await rollup.outbox(); const outbox = new Contract(outboxAddress, outboxAbi, parentProvider); const registered = (await outbox.roots(sendRoot)) !== '0x' + '0'.repeat(64); console.log('send root registered in outbox:', registered); // 5. Already claimed? console.log('outbox.isSpent(position):', await outbox.isSpent(position)); // 6. Merkle proof for a manual Outbox.executeTransaction call const nodeInterface = new Contract(NODE_INTERFACE_ADDRESS, nodeInterfaceAbi, childProvider); const proofData = await nodeInterface.constructOutboxProof(sendCount, position.toNumber()); console.log('proof root matches confirmed sendRoot:', proofData.root === sendRoot); } main(); ``` How each check maps to the lifecycle: - **`L2ToL1Tx`** (`ArbSys`, child chain): emitted at initiation. Its `position` is the withdrawal's leaf index in the send Merkle tree—the same `index` that `Outbox.executeTransaction()` and `Outbox.isSpent()` take, and the `leaf` argument to `NodeInterface.constructOutboxProof()`. The `destination`, `hash`, and `position` fields are indexed, so monitors can subscribe to them directly. - **`AssertionCreated`** and **`AssertionConfirmed`** (Rollup contract, parent chain): the assertion pipeline. A withdrawal is covered once an assertion whose child chain block has `sendCount > position` exists; it is claimable once such an assertion is _confirmed_. `AssertionConfirmed` carries the confirmed `blockHash` and `sendRoot`. You can also read `latestConfirmed()` and `getAssertion()` on the Rollup contract for point-in-time checks. For an alerting-oriented view of this pipeline (assertion cadence, missed confirmations, validator health), run the [assertion monitor](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/monitoring#assertion-monitor). - **`SendRootUpdated`** and **`roots`** (Outbox, parent chain): set by the Rollup contract at assertion confirmation. A claim can only succeed if the proof's root is registered in `roots`—this is the onchain meaning of "ready to execute." - **`OutBoxTransactionExecuted`** and **`isSpent(position)`** (Outbox, parent chain): terminal state. The event's `transactionIndex` field equals the withdrawal's `position`. - **`constructOutboxProof(size, leaf)`** (`NodeInterface`, child chain): builds the Merkle proof for a manual claim, where `size` is the confirmed block's `sendCount` and `leaf` is the withdrawal's `position`. The `NodeInterface` is a node-provided virtual contract—call it with `eth_call` against a child chain node; it doesn't exist onchain. > **Chains on the legacy (pre-BoLD) protocol** > > On chains that haven't upgraded to BoLD, the Rollup contract identifies assertions by sequential node number instead of hash, and the corresponding events are `NodeCreated` and `NodeConfirmed(nodeNum, blockHash, sendRoot)`. The `ArbSys`, `Outbox`, and `NodeInterface` surfaces are unchanged, and the SDK abstracts the difference entirely. If the parent chain is itself an Arbitrum chain (the L3 case), use the Rollup contract's `getAssertionCreationBlockForLogLookup(assertionHash)` getter to obtain block numbers suitable for event queries on the parent chain. ## Diagnose stuck withdrawals [#diagnose-stuck-withdrawals] Work through the stages in order—each row's check assumes the previous rows passed. "Phase" refers to the [bridge UI mapping](#mapping-bridge-ui-phases-to-protocol-states) above. | Symptom | Stuck at | What to check | Escalation | | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `UNCONFIRMED`, and the transaction isn't in a posted batch yet | Batch posting (phase 2, early) | `NodeInterface.getL1Confirmations(blockHash)` returns `0`, or `findBatchContainingBlock(blockNum)` reverts, for the withdrawal's child chain block | Batch poster is down or backed up—chain operator; see [batch poster troubleshooting](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/batch-poster-troubleshooting) | | `UNCONFIRMED`, batched, but no assertion covers the block | Assertion creation (phase 2) | Latest `AssertionCreated` on the Rollup contract: does the assertion's child chain block have `sendCount > position`? No recent `AssertionCreated` events at all means the active validator isn't posting | Chain operator (validator or proposer health); the [assertion monitor](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/monitoring#assertion-monitor) alerts on this automatically | | `UNCONFIRMED`, assertion created, challenge period elapsed, still no `AssertionConfirmed` | Assertion confirmation (phase 2 → 3) | Whether the assertion has a rival (a challenge is in progress—confirmation waits for resolution plus a grace period); whether any validator is calling the confirmation function at all | Chain operator; on a challenged chain, monitor the challenge and expect up to one extra challenge period plus grace period | | `CONFIRMED`, but the claim transaction reverts | Execution (phase 3) | `Outbox.isSpent(position)`—`true` means it was already claimed (find the claim via the `OutBoxTransactionExecuted` event with `transactionIndex == position`); for an L3 withdrawal, confirm you're claiming the correct leg on the correct chain; re-derive the proof with `constructOutboxProof` | If the proof root isn't in `Outbox.roots` despite `CONFIRMED` status, something is inconsistent—collect the position, child chain transaction hash, and chain ID, and contact the chain operator | | "Withdrawal is claimable, but funds never arrived" | Execution (phase 3) | Nobody executed the claim—execution is manual. Check `isSpent(position)`; if `false`, execute via the SDK or the bridge UI's **Claim** button. For token withdrawals, funds are released by the parent chain gateway to the destination address once executed | End-user cases: [bridge troubleshooting](/arbitrum-bridge/troubleshooting) | > **Historical data availability** > > Ethereum consensus nodes are required to serve blob data for only 4,096 epochs (≈18 days). Monitors that reconstruct old withdrawal history need archive access: an [archive beacon endpoint for historical blobs](/run-a-node/beacon-nodes-historical-blobs) to re-derive the chain from batch data, and an archive child chain node for the event logs that `constructOutboxProof` reads. On AnyTrust chains, the equivalent concern is the Data Availability Committee's retention window. Claiming a confirmed withdrawal itself is unaffected—proofs are built from child chain logs, not blobs. ## See also [#see-also] - [Tracing bridge transactions](/arbitrum-bridge/bridge-transaction-traceability) — follow a single deposit or withdrawal end to end - [Withdraw ETH and messages](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages) and [Withdraw tokens](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/tokens) — initiating withdrawals - [Child-to-parent messaging](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l2-to-l1-messaging) and [Assertions](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/assertions) — protocol deep dives - [Fast withdrawals](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/fast-withdrawals) and [Customizable challenge period](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/challenge-period) — chain owner configuration - [Monitoring tools for your chain](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/monitoring) — the `arbitrum-monitoring` alerting suite - [Exchange integration checklist](/launch-arbitrum-chain/integrations/exchange-integration-checklist) — deposit and withdrawal handling for exchanges - [Precompiles reference](/arbitrum-essentials/precompiles/reference) (`ArbSys`) and [NodeInterface reference](/arbitrum-essentials/nodeinterface/reference) (`constructOutboxProof`) === https://docs.arbitrum.io/how-arbitrum-works/reference/finality-and-reorgs.md (200) === # Finality and chain reorganizations (/how-arbitrum-works/reference/finality-and-reorgs) This reference explains how finality works on Arbitrum chains, why and when a chain can reorganize (reorg), how deep a reorg can go, and which confirmation level an indexer should wait for before treating data as irreversible. This is intended for developers building indexers, block explorers, bridges, and custodial integrations, and it applies to Arbitrum One, Nova, and Dedicated Blockchains (Arbitrum chains)—including AnyTrust chains that settle to another Arbitrum chain. For a step-by-step deposit and withdrawal detection procedure, see the [Exchange integration checklist](/launch-arbitrum-chain/integrations/exchange-integration-checklist). This page provides the finality and reorg model that the checklist builds on. ## The three confirmation levels [#the-three-confirmation-levels] An Arbitrum node exposes three levels of confirmation, surfaced as the standard Ethereum JSON-RPC block tags. Each maps to a different point in the transaction lifecycle and carries a different reversibility guarantee. | Level | Block tag | What it means | Can it be reverted? | | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Soft confirmation | `latest` | The Sequencer has ordered and executed the transaction and emitted it on the Sequencer feed. | Yes—this is a promise from the Sequencer, not yet backed by the parent chain. | | Parent-chain safe | `safe` | The batch containing the block has been posted to the parent chain and reached the parent chain's `safe` block. | Only by a deep parent-chain reorg. | | Parent-chain final | `finalized` | The batch containing the block has been posted to the parent chain and reached the parent chain's `finalized` block. | Only if the parent chain itself reverts a finalized block (on Ethereum, economically infeasible). | > **The load-bearing rule** > > An Arbitrum block is only as final as the parent-chain block that carries its batch. Soft confirmation is fast (sub-second) but reversible. Hard finality—the `safe` and `finalized` tags—is inherited from the parent chain and is what makes a block reorg-proof. ### The Fast Feed is not a fourth level [#the-fast-feed-is-not-a-fourth-level] On Arbitrum One, the [Fast Feed](/how-arbitrum-works/priority-gas-auction/fast-feed) publishes all transaction within the PGA round, as soon as they are ordered and executed, and before the block closes. That is earlier than `latest`, so it is tempting to treat it as the first confirmation level. Do not index against it. A Fast Feed message carries weaker guarantees than a soft confirmation: | Property | Fast Feed message | Soft confirmation (`latest`) | | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | | Block number | Tentative, not guaranteed to be final | Final for the block as sequenced | | Block hash | Absent—the block is not built yet | Present | | Inclusion | Not guaranteed; a Sequencer failure mid-block discards what it already published | The block exists and is stored | | Replay | None. You receive only messages sent after you subscribe. | Available from a node or relay | [Showing lines 1-503 of 1025 (50.0KB limit). Use offset=504 to continue.]
